body.heading: Four lives in one animal
paragraphs: Metamorphosis means change of form, and in butterflies it is total. The life cycle runs through four stages: egg, larva (the caterpillar), pupa (the chrysalis) and adult (the butterfly). Each stage is the same animal with the same DNA, rebuilt for a different job.

The caterpillar is an eating machine, devoted to growth; the butterfly is a flying, reproducing machine that may barely feed. Splitting the jobs between two bodies lets each be excellent at one thing.

body.heading: What happens inside the chrysalis
paragraphs: Inside the pupa, the caterpillar's body largely breaks down. Enzymes digest most of its tissues into a nutrient soup. But the rebuild is not from nothing: small clusters of cells called imaginal discs, present since the caterpillar stage, survive and grow rapidly into wings, legs, antennae and eyes.

After days or weeks — some species overwinter as pupae — the adult splits the case and emerges with soft, crumpled wings, pumps fluid into them to expand them, and lets them harden before its first flight. A moth does the same, but spins a silk cocoon around the pupa first. The pupa is no resting stage but the busiest of the four — a demolition and construction site inside a sealed case.

body.heading: Other ways to change
paragraphs: Butterflies, beetles, bees and flies use this complete metamorphosis. Grasshoppers and dragonflies use the incomplete kind: their young, called nymphs, look like small wingless adults and simply grow, moulting their skins, until wings appear at the final moult.
Frogs metamorphose too — a tadpole absorbs its tail, grows legs and switches from gills to lungs. In every case the logic is the same: one genome, several bodies, each fitted to a stage of life.

takeaway: Complete metamorphosis rebuilds an animal through four stages — egg, larva, pupa, adult — letting the young and adult forms live entirely different lives.
